newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest spot power weaker, Southwest firmer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest spot power weaker, Southwest firmer.

text.p: U.S. Northwest spot power prices drifted lower Wednesday on weaker demand as well as restrictions on transmission lines into California, but Southwest prices moved a bit higher, trade sources said.
"Bonneville had to lower on-peak prices with the DC (direct current) line down," said one trader.
Bonneville said capacity on the DC portion of the Intertie would be cut until Oct 20, at times to zero, for system studies by Los Angeles Department of Water & Power.
The AC (alternating current) line will also be limited next week due to scheduled maintenance.

But the crimp on supplies from the Northwest helped boost prices in the Southwest, where the unplanned outage of a southern California nuclear unit last week had already tightened supplies, trade sources said.
"You would think people would have anticipated this, but there is still a market reaction," said a California trader.
Traders also cited milder weather in both the Southwest and Northwest as a factor putting downward pressure on spot power prices.
Next-day Mid-Columbia power was last quoted $15.50-16.50 per megawatt hour (MWh), down from $18.00-19.00 on Tuesday.
California-Oregon border power was quoted $18.50-19.50, down from $19.50-20.50.
But next-day Palo Verde was quoted $21.00-22.00 per MWh, up from $20.00-21.00.
November Palo Verde was last quoted $16.25-16.60, while November COB was at $17.35-17.60.
